blocks.text: Up to now we have studied the motion of a particle along a straight line, motion in one dimension. Now consider a ball thrown horizontally from a certain height: it travels forward as well as falling downward until it strikes something such as the ground. Suppose the ball leaves the hand of the thrower at point A (Fig. 2.8a) with a velocity that is completely horizontal, vx. According to Newton's first law there is no acceleration in the horizontal direction unless a horizontally directed force acts on the ball; ignoring air friction, the only force acting during flight is gravity, so the horizontal velocity remains unchanged and equals vx until the ball hits the ground. The horizontal motion is simple: the ball moves with a constant horizontal velocity component, so the horizontal distance is x = vx t ... (2.17). The vertical motion is also uncomplicated: the ball accelerates downward under gravity, a = g, the same as a freely falling body; since the initial vertical velocity is zero, the vertical distance from Eq. 2.14 is y = (1/2) g t^2.

blocks.title: Projectiles
blocks.text: It is not necessary that an object be thrown with its initial velocity horizontal. A football kicked by a player, a ball thrown by a cricketer and a missile fired from a launching pad, all projected at some angle with the horizontal, are called projectiles. Projectile motion is two-dimensional motion under constant acceleration due to gravity.

The motion of a projectile is studied easily by resolving it into horizontal and vertical components, which are independent of each other. Suppose a projectile is fired at angle theta with the horizontal with velocity vi (Fig. 2.8b). Its components along the horizontal and vertical directions are vi cos theta and vi sin theta. The horizontal acceleration is ax = 0, because air resistance is neglected and no other force acts along this direction, whereas the vertical acceleration is ay = g. Hence the horizontal component remains constant, and at any time t, vfx = vix = vi cos theta ... (2.18). For the vertical motion the initial vertical component is vi sin theta upward; the vertical component at any instant t is found by treating the upward motion of the projectile as free fall with ay = -g, using the first equation of motion: vfy = vi sin theta - gt ... (2.19). The magnitude of the velocity at any instant is v = sqrt(vfx^2 + vfy^2) ... (2.20), and the angle phi this resultant makes with the horizontal is given by tan phi = vfy / vfx ... (2.21).

blocks.long_description: A ball thrown horizontally keeps its horizontal velocity, since no horizontal force acts, while falling vertically like a dropped ball, so its horizontal distance grows in proportion to time and its drop in proportion to the square of the time. A projectile fired at an angle has a constant horizontal component equal to the initial speed times the cosine of the angle and a vertical component that starts at the initial speed times the sine and decreases by g each second. It rises until the vertical component is zero, reaching a height proportional to the square of the initial speed and of the sine of the angle, returns to the launch level after a time of flight equal to twice the initial vertical component over g, and covers a range equal to the square of the initial speed times the sine of twice the angle over g, greatest at forty-five degrees. Air resistance shortens both the height and the range and makes the descent steeper than the ascent.

blocks.text: To find the maximum height, use the equation of motion 2aS = vf^2 - vi^2. As the body moves upward a = -g, the initial vertical velocity is viy = vi sin theta, and vfy = 0 because the body comes to rest after reaching the highest point; with S = height = h, -2gh = 0 - vi^2 sin^2 theta, or h = vi^2 sin^2 theta / (2g) ... (2.22). The height is reduced in the presence of air resistance, which decreases the upward velocity of the projectile and hence its height.

The time taken by the body to cover the distance from the place of its projection to the place where it hits the ground is the time of flight. It is obtained by taking S = h = 0, because the body goes up and comes back to the same level, covering no vertical distance. If the body is projected with velocity vi at angle theta, its vertical component is vi sin theta, and the equation of motion S = vi t + (1/2) g t^2 becomes 0 = vi sin theta t - (1/2) g t^2, so t = 2 vi sin theta / g ... (2.23), the time of flight of a projectile projected from the ground.

The maximum distance a projectile covers in the horizontal direction is its range. To find the range R, multiply the horizontal component of the velocity of projection by the total time taken to hit the ground after leaving the point of projection: R = vix x t = vi cos theta x 2 vi sin theta / g = (vi^2 / g) 2 sin theta cos theta. As 2 sin theta cos theta = sin 2theta, the range depends on the velocity and the angle of projection: R = (vi^2 / g) sin 2theta ... (2.24). For maximum range the factor sin 2theta = 1, so 2theta = sin^-1 (1) = 90 degrees, or theta = 45 degrees. For an angle less than 45 degrees the height reached and the range are both less; when the angle is larger than 45 degrees the height is more but the range is again less (Do You Know).

Air resistance slows down the forward motion of a projectile, reducing its velocity vi, and the reduction in vi decreases the range. Furthermore, air resistance is not constant throughout the flight: as the object slows down, the air resistance it experiences also decreases, so the object retards more slowly and accelerates more slowly as it falls. The result is a trajectory that is not perfectly parabolic but skewed, with a steeper descent than ascent; in the presence of air friction the trajectory of a high-speed projectile falls short of a parabolic path (For Your Information). A photograph of two balls released simultaneously, one dropped freely while the other is projected horizontally, shows the two balls at the same level at every instant: their vertical displacements are equal (Interesting Information).

blocks.title: Example 2.5
blocks.text: A ball is thrown with a speed of 30 m s^-1 in a direction 30 degrees above the horizon. Determine the height to which it rises, the time of flight and the horizontal range. Solution: vix = vi cos theta = 30 m s^-1 x cos 30 = 25.98 m s^-1; viy = vi sin theta = 30 m s^-1 x sin 30 = 15 m s^-1. Time of flight t = 2 vi sin theta / g = 2 x 15 m s^-1 / 9.8 m s^-2 = 3.1 s. Height h = vi^2 sin^2 theta / (2g) = (30 m s^-1)^2 (0.5)^2 / 19.6 m s^-2 = 11.5 m. Range R = (vi^2 / g) sin 2theta = (vi^2 / g) sin 60 = (30 m s^-1)^2 x 0.866 / 9.8 m s^-2 = 89.53 m.
